A discounted cash flow takes a growth forecast from one model and a
discount rate from another. Nothing forces the two to agree. A
general-equilibrium model derives both from one consumption process and
one set of preferences, and then prices every claim on that economy.

Long-run risks is the first family in `geap`. Consumption growth carries
a small, highly persistent component under transitory noise (Bansal and
Yaron 2004). An Epstein–Zin household prices news about that component.
A claim is a dividend process that loads on it. The loading $\phi$ is
measured from cash flows. Returns never enter the measurement. The
premium the model then prints is a prediction.

Kiku (2006) uses that structure on value and growth portfolios. Value's
dividends load more on the persistent component than growth's
($\phi = 6.2$ versus $2.6$ in Table II). The same household then
returns value's high premium and low price-dividend ratio together. The
CAPM cannot: the two legs have nearly identical market betas.

## Endowment

Four equations (Kiku 2006, eq. 6):

$$
\Delta c_{t+1} = \mu_c + x_t + \sigma_t\, \eta_{t+1}
$$

$$
x_{t+1} = \rho\, x_t + \varphi_x\, \sigma_t\, \epsilon_{t+1}
$$

$$
\sigma_{t+1}^2 = \bar\sigma^2 (1-\nu) + \nu\, \sigma_t^2 + \sigma_w\, w_{t+1}
$$

$$
\Delta d_{i,t+1} = \mu_i + \phi_i\, x_t + \varphi_{\sigma,i}\, \sigma_t\, u_{i,t+1}
$$

$x_t$ is the deviation of expected growth from its mean, a few tenths
of a percent per month, persistence $\rho = 0.98$. A shock to it is
news about the next decade of consumption. $\phi_i$ is the only
parameter that differs across claims in an economically central way.

```{python}
import geap

model = geap.LongRunRisksModel()
p = model.params
print(f"rho={p.cons.rho:g}  gamma={p.prefs.gamma:g}  psi={p.prefs.psi:g}")
for name, c in p.claims.items():
    print(f"{name:8s}  phi={c.phi:g}")
```

## Identification

Calibrate the household to consumption moments. Calibrate each claim to
its own dividend growth. Compare the returns the model was never shown.
That is the discipline. A DCF that fits a discount rate to the premium
it claims to explain cannot run the same test.

The workflow is [`LongRunRisksModel`](user-guide.qmd): specify, solve,
simulate, compare. Loadings from data go through
[`calibrate_claim`](examples.qmd). The formulas are on
[Mathematical detail](math.qmd).

## Limits

The model is an internally consistent economy, not a claim that the
economy is true.

- Return correlations in the model are too low relative to the data
  (Kiku, Table IX).
- Power utility ($\gamma = 1/\psi$) prices the value premium at zero,
  because long-run news then has no price.
- The quadrature grid is the economy you actually solve. A grid that
  truncates $x_t$ removes most of the premium. The package scales the
  quadrature weight to the unconditional distribution of $x$ so the
  nodes cover the states the process visits.
- Kiku's printed Table VII return *levels* (6.07, 11.36, 7.53 with
  $r_f = 1.58$) do not reproduce exactly from a 30-point grid. The gap
  is discretization. Spreads and betas are the objects the paper tests.

Source: Kiku (2006); Bansal and Yaron (2004); Epstein and Zin (1989).
